title: Hoisting, the temporal dead zone, and why `var` behaves differently

videos.script:
Here is a program that reads a variable on line one and declares it on line two. {{undefined}} With var, it prints undefined. With let, it stops with an error. And a function called on line one, but written at the bottom of the file, simply works.

That is hoisting. {{hoist}} Before a single line of your code runs, the engine reads the whole block and creates every name declared in it. What differs between var, let and function is what each name holds until its own line arrives.

You might never write var. {{read}} You will read it, in every codebase older than about 2016, in tutorials and in answers online. And the bug it is famous for, a loop whose callbacks all see the last value, still turns up in code reviews today.

So: {{scope}} the two kinds of scope, block and function, and which keyword lives in which. {{tdz}} The temporal dead zone, the stretch of a block where a let name exists and cannot be touched. {{loop}} The loop bug, drawn so you can see why it happens. {{globals}} And what a name declared at the top of a script does to the global object, in a browser and in Node.
